title: Ending mass atrocity and ending famine
text:
### Perspectives

## The art of medicine Ending mass atrocity and ending famine

On Sept 29, 2015, world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly adopted Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2—“end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture ending world hunger by 2030”. Meeting this goal is likely to be a complex and diffi cult undertaking: conquering endemic hunger and malnutrition will demand a raft of international policy measures for agriculture, poverty reduction, and nutrition. But one dimension of hunger in human civilisations—eliminating epidemics of starvation, namely famines—looks very hopeful. The near-abolition of great famines is a huge but unheralded achievement of our era. One of the great scourges of humanity—food crises that cause widespread hunger, disrupt society, and kill hundreds of thousands of people—are on the point of being consigned to history. There is good reason to believe that this success is driven primarily by the demise of total war and totalitarianism. It follows that eliminating famine requires further reducing armed confl ict and tyranny. Data for the decline of famine are impressive (fi gure). Between 1870 and 1969, a drumbeat of recurrent epidemic hunger killed 140 million people in 45 great and calamitous famines, defi ned as food crises that cause excess deaths of more than 100 000 and 1 million people, respectively. During the 1970s and 1980s, 5·4 million people died in famines, including the last two calamitous famines on record— Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge in the late 1970s and Ethiopia in 1984–85. In the past 25 years, that fatal drumbeat has faded. There have been just six great famines since 1990, which in total have killed some 1·4 million people, about half of them North Koreans—a cumulative death toll equivalent to the yearly average of the century before 1970. The 2015 edition of the Global Hunger Index was published this month. Its headline is that since the millennium, chronic undernourishment has declined substantially, but that more than 50 countries face severe challenges if SDG 2 on ending hunger by 2030 is to be achieved. Its other powerful message is that famines are all but eradicated. This fi nding draws on a database of famines since 1870. Building upon the work of many scholars in this fi eld, notably Stephen Devereux, Paul Howe, and Cormac Ó Gráda, the historical catalogue also includes episodes of deliberate mass starvation such as in war or genocide. As with world changes on this scale, there are no simple explanations for this decline in famines. Shares of the credit can credibly be claimed by huge increases in global incomes and agricultural productivity, and by transport and informational advances. Great strides in global public health are particularly striking. A century ago, communicable diseases, such as smallpox, measles, and waterborne infections, were major contributors to famine death tolls—and there can be no doubt that immunisation campaigns, improved water and sanitation, and better primary health care have made food crises far less lethal than before. This combination of factors is most obvious in China, which suff ered about half of the world’s famine deaths until the 1960s, and has since posted spectacular rates of economic growth and human development. As world population has grown, from about 1·3 billion in 1870 to 7·3 billion today, famines have become rarer. Malthusians who fear that rising population will inevitably provoke gigantic famine are not winning the argument. Climate change will undoubtedly have serious eff ects on food systems across the world, but so far it has not reversed the downward trend in famine incidence. Politics is also part of the story. The economist Amartya Sen famously suggested that democratic freedoms should be seen as the real force behind the elimination of famine. He argued that while India saw a marked reduction in famine after independence in 1947, China suff ered the worst famine in recorded history in 1958–62, costing an estimated 30 million lives. India’s vigilant press reported on imminent food crises and its parliamentarians called government to account. By contrast, severe censorship and repression during Mao Zedong’s Great Leap Forward meant that one of the greatest catastrophes of the 20th century was not even acknowledged until well after Mao’s death. And worldwide, the increase in democracy and press freedoms in many countries also correspond with diminishing famine.

Any causal explanation needs not only a general correlation, but also a plausible account for each specifi c instance. Each of the 58 famines since 1870 has a clearly identifi able political or military contributing factor, and as we move to the more recent examples, those political causes become increasingly prominent. In premodern agrarian societies, harvest failure due to drought or pest infestation could bring devastating hunger in its wake. In the industrial-colonial era, the violence of imperial subjugation undermined the resilience of peoples in aff ected countries. When natural adversities such as El Niño cycles intersected with colonial policies that dismantled livelihoods, the result was what writer Mike Davis has called “late Victorian Holocausts” across India and China, culminating in the Chinese famine of 1907, which is estimated to have killed about 24 million people. African famines were comparably terrible, but because of the continent’s smaller population, killed fewer people overall. From World War 1 to the fall of the Berlin Wall—the short 20th century—immediate political factors come to the fore. In this era, starvation was overwhelmingly caused by governments that waged total war, infl icted genocide, or pursued totalitarian social engineering. In the 30 years after the Russian Revolution, perhaps 22 million Europeans— mainly Russians, Ukrainians, and Poles living in the continent’s breadbasket—died in famines created by communists, Nazis, or both. The worst episodes were the Russian civil war, Stalin’s forced collectivisation known to Ukrainians as the Holodomor, and the Nazi “Hunger Plan” for eastern Europe in World War 2, which aimed to reduce the population of Poland and the western Soviet Union by some 30 million people and starved an estimated 4·2 million people. The Netherlands’ “Hunger Winter” of 1944 claimed fewer lives, but showed that even people in economically developed countries could still be reduced to starvation under duress. Asian famines killed still higher numbers, including the starvation in Indonesia, Vietnam, and then Bengal during World War 2, and Mao’s Great Leap Forward famine. Cambodia’s Year Zero (1·75 million dead from hunger during 1975–79) and the North Korean famine of 1995–97 (600 000 deaths) show how this deadly legacy of totalitarianism lived on after Mao’s death. Africa is again a diff erent version of the main story. The two African famines that approached a million fatalities were the Nigerian civil war in 1967–70, which was caused by war and blockade of the Biafran enclave, and Ethiopia during 1983–85 when war and drought lethally intersected. Since 1990—with the anomaly of North Korea—famines have largely been caused by armed confl icts. There have been two such war episodes in Somalia. In 1992, the cause was the depredation of armed factions fi ghting over the ruins of the state. In 2011–12, it was drought and war. That recent famine could have been averted by prompt humanitarian action, but restrictions on international relief agencies providing assistance in places controlled by the group al-Shabaab, designated as a terrorist organisation by the US Government, meant that action was too little and too late to save the lives of about 250 000 Somalis, mostly children. In Darfur, the Sudanese Government’s assault on a civilian population identifi ed as rebels caused at least 200 000 deaths from hunger and disease between 2003 and 2006. Meanwhile, in Syria today, deaths from hunger have yet to reach the 100 000 threshold, but there are pockets of extreme hunger in besieged towns, and a near-total denial of humanitarian aid in areas controlled by the Islamic State. As with the Somali famine, the resources and technology for eff ective famine response exist—but are not used. Overall, decade by decade, as the number and lethality of wars have declined, so too have associated famines. Today’s most destructive wars are causing the collapse of the social order and mass migration across a vast swathe of the greater Middle East—but not millions of famine deaths. Too often, famines and mass atrocities that involve forced starvation have been studied separately. Specialists in food and agriculture tend not to analyse war and genocide. Scholars of mass atrocity focus on violent killing, and have not analysed mass death from the perspective of starvation and disease. International criminal prosecutors have concerned themselves with direct violence—murder, torture, and rape—avoiding the question of culpability for starvation. Humanitarians alone have tried to combine the analysis of famine and atrocity, but theirs has been an isolated voice in the academy. The 2015 Global Hunger Index suggests a variant on Sen’s hypothesis: as colonialism, total war, and totalitarian rule came to an end, so did great and calamitous famines. Every one of the great and calamitous famines since the early 20th century was a deliberate act, committed by individuals who were ready to destroy—or at least to tolerate the destruction of—entire populations. There are many close parallels with mass killing of civilians: it is often the very same perpetrators, with the same sets of goals, and the same attitude to the lives of innocent people. Similarly, the background factors that make it more diffi cult to perpetrate mass atrocity—the interconnectedness of the world, a consensus that it is unacceptable to allow whole populations to be sacrifi ced, and people’s awareness of their rights and readiness to mobilise to defend them—are the same that have reduced famine crimes. The elimination of famine requires greater eff orts at preventing and resolving deadly confl icts, and fewer hindrances on providing humanitarian assistance in those confl icts that do occur. There can be no excuses for famine.
